2QA: When Emergency SOS button is tapped and Continue is tapped on the confirmation dialog , and there is no prior active incident id, a new incident is created when calling /driver/safety/emergencyAssist/requestExternalHelp endpoint. This opens Please stand by screen.

If the incident creation is successful, the incident id is returned in the response which is locally saved. 

On successful incident creation, ThirdPartyIncidentService polls /driver/safety/emergencyAssist/requestExternalHelpUpdate endpoint, until it receives any error from BE (may be server error or when incident is closed)

When the app is killed and relaunched, it resumes polling if active incident id is present in driver setting. This incident id will be cleared(set to 0) when any error is obtained from hitting /driver/safety/emergencyAssist/requestExternalHelpUpdate endpoint

Safety toolkit bottom sheet's Emergency assist entry opens Please stand by screen when an active incident is present

Nice speaking with you earlier, this looks like a great initiative!

As discussed, if you can please attach the spreadsheets you showed me with the greater detail of our insurance offering to drivers this will assist our legal analysis moving forward. 

As for next steps, if you can please clarify for me how we anticipate this insurance to be provided and what coverage we want out of it would be great. What I need here is, how it will apply in practice from your view, so for example a driver signs onto the platform and completes 200 hours then they get a notification that says ‘Hey X, as a regular Bolt driver you are now eligible for Y’?. This will need to be stress tested with the Gabrielle matter and I can pick this up with [~accountid:5acb1f48d8b95a2b34f150a8] but I don't know if its the best idea not offering it to all drivers in the first instance otherwise this would go against our promise of offering better working conditions for all drivers etc. Happy to hear your view on this though as this will assist. 

Appreciating also that you mentioned that this insurance will only be provided while the driver is “on trip” which is useful for our purposes, but we will need to ensure this is well documented and mirrored within all of our insurance documents as well as applied in a practical sense - I can help you with this once the below review is complete/cleared from a legal standpoint. 

*The key questions I have is:* 

# What does the current driver and bolt insurance cover (separate to the insurance above and what each driver has now)? For example if a passenger is injured while on trip with a driver or getting out of a vehicle - does their existing insurance cover this already or will the new insurance cover this? 
# Or is the new insurance offering only intended to cover the driver which fills the gap in their existing insurance that is provided? (Has there been complaints from drivers where they werent covered by insurance for incidents). Just need clarity on what parties are covered and to what extent.
# Once we know what our existing insurance covers and what the new insurance would seek to cover, it would be good to understand how it will be applied in practice and what the reasoning is behind the 200 hours of service required first and why is it not instantly applied when a driver joins our platform etc. 

Do reach out if you need me to clarify anything, once we have the above information we will have a fuller picture to complete a review for you. 

Have a good week. 

Many thanks, 

Clarissa

I would like to comment on the use of Bolt marks by this new supplier (and the use of Bolt marks in general). 

Bolt marks, as defined in our [https://bolt.eu/en/brand/guidelines/|https://bolt.eu/en/brand/guidelines/|smart-link], is our most valued asset that we are growing meticulously. We can allow to use our brand if there is a clear benefit for our brand and for us as company as per our IP strategy. By giving the right to use our brand we also need to weigh any possible accompanying image risks. The use of our brand is subject to sign-off by legal, procurement and our brand team. Overall process is described here: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3922232082/Bolt+Brand+Guidelines+a+practical+perspective|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3922232082/Bolt+Brand+Guidelines+a+practical+perspective|smart-link]

With the specific case, we have not worked with this supplier previously; the supplier has only recently been established; we are just exploring the possibilities to cooperate with them, i.e this is a pilot project not a long-term relationship. As a rule, we have not allowed use of our brand by our suppliers. Especially without proven track record, and definitely not allowed this to newly established companies as the image risks are way higher that possible benefit.

Also, I do not see any benefit here for Bolt brand as such (small discount does not constitute such in situation where there are plenty of other similar companies that could equally do the same for us). I only see a possibility for the newly established company, with whom we have not yet established any cooperation nor proven track record, to benefit from our name and image.

To wrap up, the preconditions for allowing the use of our brand have not been met, and we cannot sign of the use of our brand in this specific case.

This message has been aligned with procurement team and follows previous guidelines given by the brand team.

Please let me know if you still have any further questions.

 

BR

Marja-Liisa

amatia.lomax: For each ride we estimate the coefficient of motor force vs forward acceleration (i.e. how much force was required to cause a certain increase in speed). This coefficient is a proxy for mass of the rider.

We compare this coefficient (for a given incoming ride) with the previous coefficients for a given user ID; if new_coefficient > 1.4 (threshold now increased to 1.5) x historic_median_coefficient we predict tandem = True and send a push notification.

In this case, I can see that this particular ride has a much higher coefficient than previous rides for this user.

--k.issuer,
k.types,
k.driver_id AS driver,
--- 

COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.order_id END) AS count_bad_orders,
COUNT(DISTINCT k.order_id) AS count_all_orders,
SUM(CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.rider_price_eur END) AS sum_bad_rides,
SUM(k.rider_price_eur) AS sum_all_rides,
COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.order_id END)*1.00/COUNT(DISTINCT k.order_id) AS count_ratio,
SUM(CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.rider_price_eur END)*1.00/SUM(k.rider_price_eur) AS sum_ratio
FROM (
SELECT 
etl.order_id AS order_id,
etl.country_code AS order_country,
ot.driver_id AS driver_id,
etl.card_variant AS card_variant,
etl.user_price_eur AS rider_price_eur,
CASE WHEN (etl.is_payment_problem OR etl.is_chargeback OR etl.is_final_failed_payment) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END as bad_payment_order
FROM 
ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl 
JOIN ng_public.company_order AS co ON etl.order_id = co.id AND etl.city_id = co.city_id
JOIN ng_public.company_order_try ot ON etl.order_id = ot.order_id AND etl.city_id = ot.city_id 
LEFT JOIN ng_public.user_user as uu on uu.id = etl.user_id
WHERE 
etl.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) as date)
AND co.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) as date)
AND ot.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, current_date) as date)
AND etl.order_type = 'rides'
AND etl.order_try_state = 'finished'
AND etl.payment_method_group = 'in-app'

---

AND etl.card_variant NOT IN ('visa','mastercard')
AND etl.country_code = 'fr'
--AND fdr.status = 'active'
--AND etl.country_code = 'gb'
AND etl.user_price_eur > 600
--AND etl.payment_method_type = 'adyen_paypal'
AND DATE_DIFF('day',uu.created, etl.created) < 10
--AND DATE_DIFF('day',uu.created, etl.created) < 30
--AND ot.distance < 200
		AND ot.ride_distance > 120000
GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5,6

) AS k 
GROUP BY 1
/*
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.order_id END) > 30
HAVING
COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.order_id END) >= 2 
--AND SUM(CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.rider_price_eur END) > 100
AND 
((COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.order_id END)*1.00/COUNT(DISTINCT k.order_id)) > 0.3
OR 
(SUM(CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.rider_price_eur END)*1.00/SUM(k.rider_price_eur)) > 0.6)
AND SUM(CASE WHEN k.bad_payment_order = 1 THEN k.rider_price_eur END) > 500
*/
ORDER BY 7 DESC
LIMIT 50{code}

{code:sql}INSERT INTO way_nodes (way_id, node_id, version, sequence_id)
    SELECT  way_id, node_id, version, sequence_id
    FROM current_way_nodes wn
    INNER JOIN current_ways w
    ON wn.way_id = w.id
    WHERE id = ANY(... new way ids here ...){code}



The difference is that in the 1936 ways case, the Query Planner chooses to not use the {{current_way_nodes}} index {{"current_way_nodes_pkey" PRIMARY KEY, btree (way_id, sequence_id)}}.

This is the faulty query plan (note the Seq Scan):

Hi Taisiia, 

Thank you for raising this issue, I have reviewed the proposal and here are my thoughts.

Some issues with this process:

* Regulatory issues - I’m not sure about the UK, but in EE it’s a law that the driver’s legal name must be displayed in the app, so adding this info contradicts this. We should use the same solution in every market, and this would not be possible with the suggested process
* In the UK/EU markets, there might be issues with this falling under personal data under the GDPR , though I’m not 100% sure here
* I imagine doesn't look great in the app - it’s a hacky solution
* If a product solution is later implemented, you'd have to go back through the profiles and remove the info from the name, and I’m sure that in the markets where we’re following this process, we don’t have lists of drivers whose names we changed to include this info…
* By doing this, we avoid pushing for a real solution from product.

I agree that having this info in the app would be valuable for our drivers - I can imagine a scenario where a rider tries to call a driver who is hard of hearing via the app, but the driver doesn’t answer/hangs up, and the rider assumes they are being rude by not responding. 

However, I think the cons of this idea outweigh the pros, and I would suggest that other markets don’t do this either, especially as it’s not a documented process! 

Additionally, I think if we had a real solution in the app, then this could encourage people to become Bolt drivers, as we’d be more inclusive and supportive of those with a disability. 

Until a product solution is explored, we can encourage drivers to display a sign in their vehicle, if they wish, to inform riders. I have experienced this here in Estonia, where a driver had a sign in her vehicle advising that she was hard of hearing. 

I’ll close this ticket, but happy to support you if you decide to suggest this as an idea in the rider app - perhaps you can suggest it in #rider-app-feedback?

Hi [~accountid:610d3190ae72b2006f81ee2e],

Please find below the external counsel’s advice:



              *_we are obliged to pay the above-mentioned benefits or if they should be paid exclusively by the agencies?_*

*_ML:_* _They should be paid exclusively by the agencies._

_Bolt Portugal entered into service agreements (outsourcing) with the referred agencies by which the latter undertook to provide a specific service and, as such, allocate its employees (the pickers) to the execution of the services. For the provision of such services, Bolt Portugal pays a monthly price/fees to such agencies._

_The pickers are employees of the service providers (i.e. of Jobandtalent and Randstad). All the benefits and payments referred in the e-mail below are due under Portuguese labour law and arise from the existence of an employment relationship between such employees and their employers (the referred agencies). There is no obligation of ensuring such payments since Bolt Portugal is not the employer of the individuals allocated to the provision of the services. Such payments and the remaining labour obligations must be complied with by the agencies, as employers. Bolt Portugal is only obliged to pay the price/fees agreed in the respective service agreements for the provision of the services._

_The price/fees agreed for the services usually already take into account the costs of the service provider, namely with human resources._

_Please note that this is expressly stated in both drafts of service agreements at stake in which is clear that Bolt Portugal does not assume any charges with the human resources of the service providers allocated to the services, which are the sole responsibility of the latter, being such employees paid by their employers, that also pay the respective contributions to the Social Security as well as the work accidents insurance (please see clause 4 of the service agreements at stake)._

              *_paying such benefits puts us at risk of illegal assignment of employees?_*

*_ML:_* _Yes, it increases such risk. There are no legal constraints to a company providing services to another company under a service agreement entered into between them. This situation is lawful provided that the employees of the service provider perform their work under the supervision and direction of the service provider (their employer) and not under the supervision and direction of the beneficiary of the activity (in this case, Bolt Portugal)._

_The payments referred in the e-mail below are due under an employment relationship and, therefore, must be ensured by the agencies, as employers of such employees (and not by Bolt Portugal). Otherwise, there might be a risk of these employees claiming to have an employment relationship with Bolt Portugal - although they are formally hired by the outsourcing service providers - and obtain recognition from a labour court of their employment to the company to which the services are being provided (Bolt Portugal)._

_Even if such payments are made by Bolt Portugal to the agencies (and not directly to the employees at stake) – which seems to be the case at stake - in practice, all the labour costs with such employees are being borne by Bolt Portugal. This increases the risk identified above since it may be an additional argument to allege that the “real” employment relationship is between Bolt Portugal and the pickers, being the agencies only the “formal employers”._

_This means that in case of termination of the employment contract by the agencies, employees might challenge the dismissal based on the argument that they have an employment relationship with Bolt Portugal (and not with the agencies). Furthermore, the situation at stake may be deemed as an illegal assignment of employees which constitutes a very serious labour infraction, punishable with the payment of a fine (this last risk exists in case of an inspection by the Portuguese Labour Authority which may occur randomly or due to an employee’s claim)._



In summary, the picker benefits must be paid exclusively by the agencie. Moreover, Bolt Portugal must not pay any benefits to avoid risks of illegal assignment of employees.



Should you have any further questions, please do let me know.

Thank you.

Hi [~accountid:6033825e8ff0980071452fc9] thank you for your input. I understand the frustration but I wouldn’t call our responsibility to do our due diligence in data protection compliance and protecting the privacy of our users a bureaucracy. 

The responsibility of answering to police request is the responsibility of support team. If in Poland some other process has been agreed to, then this is between the respective teams to figure out to make things flow smoother. The guidelines from the Safety team as we have properly documented trail and central control over what data is being released: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4040950288/Requests+from+Authorities+or+Police|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4040950288/Requests+from+Authorities+or+Police|smart-link].  If there are any issues with that, these can also be raised with them. 

Regarding the content of the request, just based on the info in this one and not having seen the actual original request, it is still extremely vague and we just cannot release data based on this. We've a standard response that we usually use in this instances: 

_We trust you understand that any disclosure of personal data from Bolt for law enforcement purposes must still comply with the GDPR, and in particular a lawful basis is required at Art.6. The disclosure must be necessary and proportionate to the stated purpose._ 

_Bolt cannot lawfully disclose this information only having been told that the purpose concerns an "investigation". With no details having been provided, Bolt cannot undertake nor document an assessment for lawful disclosure - as required by law. The threshold of criminality is unknown, and so any test for necessity and proportionality is made impossible._ 

_What's more, the request also seeks travel data, including pick-up and drop-off locations, which likely constitute 'personal data' of third parties as understood by the GDPR. In the disclosure request, no link was mentioned between those data points with criminal activity, and the purpose beyond the "investigation". The potential, even inadvertent, loss of those third party's right to privacy must be warranted in these circumstances, and the use or intention of that data upon disclosure explained (at least at high level)._

_In short, compliance with the current disclosure request conflicts with other legal obligations with which Bolt is required to comply i.e. data protection._

_Bolt has a dedicated function and support staff to manage such enquiries which are handled under the strictest of confidence. Should you wish to share the criminal activity associated with the investigation, and demonstrate (at a high level) why the loss of privacy in this instance is warranted and required to assist in that investigation, then please do let us know._

This is an example of an XSLT code that SHOULD return “12”. Using that, we could generate a “Payment_Terms_ID” as they should all be “Net_” and then the number.

eg: Net 18 = Net_18



Immediate Analysis:

* We would get errors if Telema tries to upload using a Net_X where this ID doesn’t exist (eg Net_55).
* We would have to create another hashmap, or another integration mapping, to cover the checking against existing Net_X payment terms. These would have to be managed when new are updated, and rules should be in place for when the payment term does not match one of these.
* We would have to test cases surrounding leap years.
* We will have to check if we can update Payment Terms using the API (probably, but still good to check)

h2. Due Date overwritten Payment Terms

The Due date value in Telema already auto-calculates the Payment term, which would allow us to simply overwrite the due-date in workday with the Telema due date, rather than consider the Payment Term at all (from an integration perspective).

Query for high level data:

{noformat}SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', etl.created) AS "month"
	,etl.country_code
	,count(etl.order_id) AS count_all_orders
	,sum(etl.partner_price_eur) AS sum_all_orders
	,ROUND(COUNT(CASE 
				WHEN etl.fraud_label = TRUE
					THEN etl.order_id
				ELSE NULL
				END), 0) AS count_of_fraud
	,ROUND(SUM(CASE 
				WHEN etl.fraud_label = TRUE
					THEN etl.partner_price_eur
				ELSE 0
				END), 0) AS sum_of_fraud
	,ROUND(COUNT(CASE 
				WHEN etl.fraud_label = TRUE
					THEN etl.order_id
				ELSE NULL
				END) * 1.0 / COUNT(etl.order_id), 4) AS fraud_count_ratio
	,ROUND(SUM(CASE 
				WHEN etl.fraud_label = TRUE
					THEN etl.partner_price_eur
				ELSE 0
				END), 0) * 1.0 / SUM(partner_price_eur) AS fraud_sum_ratio - ROUND(SUM(CASE 
				WHEN etl.fraud_label = TRUE
					THEN etl.partner_price_eur
				ELSE 0
				END), 0) * 1.0 / SUM(partner_price_eur) AS fraud_sum_ratio
FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders etl
LEFT JOIN archive_analytical.delivery_order_request dor ON dor.id = etl.fraud_calculation_id
	AND dor.created_hour >= DATE ('2022-06-01')
CROSS JOIN UNNEST(dor.strategies) AS strat
WHERE etl.created_date >= DATE ('2022-06-01')
	AND etl.order_type = 'food_delivery'
	AND etl.order_state = 'finished'
	AND strat."name" LIKE '%VERIFIED_MAN%'
--and etl.order_id in (94324665)
GROUP BY 1
	,2
ORDER BY 2
	,1 DESC{noformat}

*Findings*: 

As it can seen below, the findings suggest that the highest frequency of false positive cases occur in South Africa, Ghana and Kenya.

!Screenshot 2022-12-08 at 16.29.28.png|width=923,height=417!

After testing various thresholds based on elements from our input, in order to no longer enable the verified fraudsters, most results had a high false positive rate. 

The next step was narrowing the fraud score of these users at the moment of the fraud calculation, in order to see who would be affected by a small adjustment of the fraud score attributed to the rule (from -201 to -200) – namely those users that had *fraud score=99* at the time of ordering. 

We tested this modification on the following 6 markets: ZA,KE,GH,MT,EE,AZ. We found that  implementing this change in South Africa and Ghana would yield high savings (1470 eur in ZA // 1581 eur in GH), covering a significant part of the true negatives missed through this rule, while maintaining an acceptable amount of good GMV loss by false positive ratios (42.78% in ZA // 38.66% in GH). Additionally, the coverage of true negative in Ghana is almost 50% by adjusting the fraud score of this from from -201 to -200.

!Screenshot 2022-12-08 at 16.48.32.png|width=1317,height=163!

*Actions*:

Based on these findings, the action implemented was the adjusted of the fraud score attributed to rule EATER_VERIFIED_MANUALLY from -201 to -200 in Ghana and South Africa.

Hey!

The main principle to follow is that only personal data that is related to make the recruitment decision based on the role shall be asked. This means that any questions asked must be related and justified due to the specific role which the candidate is applying to. Therefore we always have to be ready to explain how the question relates to the role the person is applying to. 

Special categories of data should not be asked. These are questions regarding the following: 

* racial or ethnic origin,
* political opinions, 
* religious or philosophical beliefs, 
* trade union membership, 
* genetic data, 
* biometric data,
* health,
* natural person's sex life or sexual orientation.

In general the following topics should also be avoided:

* any question regarding private life, e.g. kids, marital status
* age

I hope this helps in formulating the guidelines!

Liis

Team, here are conclusions:

There are likely no obstacles to issuing invoice on behalf of one person and making the payout to another person under the local laws, BUT we strongly don’t recommend doing that for the following reasons:

* We might be facilitating money laundering if the payout is not made to the invoice issuer - we already got in a huge mess because of that in Latvia (one of our employees is under criminal investigation - accused of facilitating tax evasion by using proxies aka making fleet payouts to private persons). Banks can ask for additional documentation regarding the payments facilitated by us; failing to provide sufficient evidence (_agreement_) can lead to suspension of services.
*  We might incur problems with the tax authorities who will be unable to properly levy taxes on the relevant income of the drivers/fleets. Bolt may be held responsible for aiding and abetting or even orchestrating a tax fraud.
* Our Driver T&Cs state that we are making the payouts to the contractual party. If we are making the payouts to any other person / entity, it should be clearly agreed via a separate agreement.
* We currently don’t have a finred license to remit money. We can get away with it only if the financial service provided by ourselves fits under one of available licensing exemptions. The exemption we use applies only if we are remitting money on behalf of just one payer or payee (not both). If invoice is issued by one player and the payout is made to another player, then we are basically not remitting money on behalf of one player.

CASE WHEN oc.ride_duration*2 < oc.ride_duration THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS small_ride_duration_against_prediction,
pop.distance as est_predicted_distance,
CASE WHEN (opc.paid_wait_day_component + opc.paid_wait_night_component) > 0 AND (ROUND ((ot.ride_price/r.rate),2)) > (ROUND(pop.predicted_price / r.rate, 2)) AND ((great_circle_distance(oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lat,oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lng,oc.driving_with_client_lat,oc.driving_with_client_lng)*1000) ) > 150 AND ((((great_circle_distance(oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lat,oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lng,oc.lat,oc.lng))*1000)) > 150 OR (((great_circle_distance(oc.lat,oc.lng,oc.driving_with_client_lat,oc.driving_with_client_lng))*1000)) > 500) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS fraudulent_order_flag -- wait > drive
from glue.ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl 
left join glue.ng_public.company_order_try as ot on ot.order_id = etl.order_id and ot.city_id = etl.city_id 
left join glue.ng_public.etl_order_pricing_components as opc on opc.order_id = etl.order_id and opc.city_id = etl.city_id 
left join glue.ng_public.fraud_order_check as oc on oc.order_id = etl.order_id and oc.city_id = etl.city_id 
LEFT JOIN glue.ng_public.pricing_order_prediction as pop on pop.order_id=etl.order_id and pop.city_id = etl.city_id
left join glue.ng_public.vw_currency_exchange_rates AS r ON r.currency = ot.price_currency and cast(r.valid_on as date) = cast(etl.created as date)
--where ot.driver_id = 3184909
where ot.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('week', -2, current_date) as date)
and etl.created >= CAST(DATE_ADD('week', -2, current_date) as date)
and ot.state = 'finished'
and etl.order_state = 'finished'
and etl.order_try_state = 'finished'
AND etl.order_type = 'rides'
and etl.country_code = 'se'
AND pop.next_prediction_id IS null
--and (CASE WHEN (opc.paid_wait_day_component + opc.paid_wait_night_component) > 0 AND (ROUND ((ot.ride_price/r.rate),2)) > (ROUND(pop.predicted_price / r.rate, 2)) AND ((great_circle_distance(oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lat,oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lng,oc.driving_with_client_lat,oc.driving_with_client_lng)*1000) ) > 150 AND ((((great_circle_distance(oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lat,oc.driver_arrived_to_client_lng,oc.lat,oc.lng))*1000)) > 150 OR (((great_circle_distance(oc.lat,oc.lng,oc.driving_with_client_lat,oc.driving_with_client_lng))*1000)) > 500) THEN 1 ELSE 0 end) = 1
order by ot.driver_id, etl.created, etl.order_id)
select distinct x.driver,
count (distinct case when x.fraudulent_order_flag = 1 then x.orders end) as wait_fee_orders,
count(distinct x.orders) as all_orders,
((count (distinct case when x.fraudulent_order_flag = 1 then x.orders end)) * 1.00)/ count(distinct x.orders) AS ratio
from x as x
group by 1
order by 1{code}

Tested the second idea with some changes, and it works fine. Prepared prototype for sredb pypi repo. 
So what we have. 
1. All requests to artifactory has format: {{ url }}/artifactory/{{ repository_name }}/others_systems_fields

Based on this I created 2 local repositories in jfrog: sredb-pypi-internal/sredb-pypi-external

!image-20221209-124713.png|width=1768,height=679!

2. Changed configuration for public domain of envoy to: 

{noformat}              - name: jfrog-artifactory.prelive.bolt.eu
                domains: ["jfrog-artifactory.prelive.bolt.eu"]
                routes:
                - match:
                    safe_regex:
                      google_re2: {}
                      regex: ".*external.*"
                  route:
                    append_x_forwarded_host: true
                    cluster: artifactory-api
                  request_headers_to_add:
                    - header:
                        key: X-JFrog-Override-Base-Url
                        value: "https://jfrog-artifactory.prelive.bolt.eu"{noformat}

So here, for public domains, we accept requests only to the path which contains the word *external*. So here according to name conviction, we should remember, that anonymous access should have access to repos which has “external“ in the name. Potentially, we may specify the whole repo name like *.*sredb-pypi-external*.* So this approach also has benefits, that we close the access to everything except these repos via public. 

3. Here I tried to upload package via public endpoint: [https://jfrog-artifactory.prelive.bolt.eu/artifactory/api/pypi/sredb-pypi-external|https://jfrog-artifactory.prelive.bolt.eu/artifactory/api/pypi/sredb-pypi-external] , and it works, no issues with that. For uploading, I created a user who has only write permissions only to this repo and used the credentials of this user. 

!image-20221209-125152.png|width=955,height=294!

4. After that I enabled replication for repository sredb-pypi-external to sredb-pypi-internal, it’s event based replication, so once a new artifact is indexed in external repo, it took less the second to become available in sredb-pypi-internal repositories. 

5. After that, I enabled anonymous access, allow anonymous read-only to sredb-pypi-internal, and tried to search the package anonymously via our internal endpoint: [https://jfrog-artifactory.prelive.boltint.net/artifactory/api/pypi/sredb-pypi-internal/simple|https://jfrog-artifactory.prelive.boltint.net/artifactory/api/pypi/sredb-pypi-internal/simple] 

P.S. simple here, it’s required only for pip. 

!image-20221209-125753.png|width=1075,height=693!

And artifacts was found: 

!image-20221209-125814.png|width=948,height=110!

Summary: 

# We need to use name scheme:

*  repos with public access should contains: external in name 
* repos with public access should contains: internal in name 

2. If need to provide internal access to these repos, we need to enable replication from external to internal repos.
P.S. It’s not our main case, so here I assume that we not going to consume to much space in s3. But if needs we may use some ways to autoclean external repositories by cron (due to we have replicas in internal repo). 

3. Anonymous access, shouldn’t allow everything in artifactory, we must to specify it for each repo where it requires. 

4. For such cases where we need public access to repo, we should use 2 endpoints (1 internal/1 external).

+*Copy of the email sent today 9 Dec to OC*+:

Dear Claire, Jerome and Chloé,

I am reverting on the Branded Cars Program risk assessment - thanks again for this. We have now had the opportunity to consider all options with the Business and I am coming back to you with some clarification questions as well as some suggestions, where I would need your input please, before we decide what Phase 2 of this assignment will look like (i.e. new contract or revised T&Cs with opt-in form for instance).

*Envisaged solutions* and *questions*:

As you will see in the mark-up, our main questions relate to the implications that would arise from treating the driver as an advertiser service provider - hence our proposal instead to adopt better worded T&Cs accompanied by an opt-in form and a monthly remuneration, if this decreases sufficiently the reclassification risks associated with the Program. I set out below our main questions and reasoning but it might be easier to follow our reasoning in the document itself (mark-up attached):

* +OC proposal / Solution 2:+ The driver becomes a media owner and signs a specific agreement (advertising space purchase contract) with Bolt (acting as advertiser) whereby he accepts specific conditions related to the remuneration and the advertising. 

This becomes clearly an advertising service provided by the driver - which raises the following questions on our side please: 

-_-> New service provided by the driver:_

* What does that entail on his side? Is there no risk for the driver to proceed like this?
* Does he have to set-up anything else than his usual company / his current way of providing VTC services?
* Does he need to have a separate entity or to have a specific NACE code?
* Do we need to inform the driver? Guide them about any changes required?

-_-> New contract to be signed by driver and Bolt:_

* Can the driver just sign an advertising contract drafted by Bolt (without any option really to negotiate it)?
* Could we add a disclaimer in the contract, to ensure that the liability of proceeding like this lies with the driver, not Bolt?
* Is it ok if BOLT presents the same contract template to each driver?

_--> Invoicing:_ 

* Drivers are not trained/equipped to issue invoices. This is also one of the reasons why they would choose to ride on a platform, as the platform issues the trips' invoices on their behalf.

* What would be the risk of Bolt issuing the invoice for that service on behalf of the driver (we would add a provision in the Advertising Contract authorizing us to do so)?

* Could the monthly fee (+ rétro-commission) be paid to the drivers by Bolt as a bonus - i.e. without the driver issuing an invoice for that service?

* +Bolt counter-proposal / Solution 3+ (based on OC risk assessment of current existing Programme / Solution 1) : We would prefer to keep a mechanism close to the current one, but we would update the T&Cs and add an opt-in form, whereby the driver (and if needed, Bolt) would sign and that would also record the starting date of the advertising for each driver. We would envisage the following changes to the Program, to mitigate the risks highlighted in your Memo:

* we could explain that we rent the driver's 2 advertising spaces on their car (if that helps, we could also say that they remain free to have other logos or advertisements inside the car for instance);

* we would limit the Program to either 1 year max or 6 months renewable once, with the possibility for the driver and Bolt to terminate upon 1 month notice;

* we would pay the driver a fixed monthly + a retro-commission: each driver who is a Bolt Ambassadeur would get 100€ per month (= fixed amount) + 9% commission kickback on any Bolt rides made during the previous month (= incentive) (+ eventually, a one-time bonus of 250€ paid after 4 months of having the sticker, if we need to encourage more drivers to join the Program);

* we would detail all the above in revised T&Cs and would have an opt-in form, where the driver would acknowledge the T&Cs for the Programme Ambassadeur, sign and date (Bolt could also sign, if needed).

--> If we were to proceed as described above ("Solution 3"), could you please advise where that would leave us in terms of reclassification risks? Would you say we would be closer to 10-15% risks of reclassification and perhaps 30% in terms of risk of contractual imbalance?

We really hope to be able to proceed with *Solution 3*, which *seems easier from a driver's experience perspective* - even though there are still a few points we'd need to clarify, such as the invoicing point (nb: If it turns out that the bonus system is not a viable option and the driver has to issue monthly invoices to Bolt for the advertising services, even if we implement Solution 3, that raises a number of issues as we're not sure the drivers could do this + there's also the question of applicable VAT, as the VAT for advertisement services might be different from the one for ride-hailing services).

In any case, Solution 3 seems to be easier for Bolt to put in place and easier for the drivers as well - bearing in mind that our target for next year is to have 5000 'chauffeurs ambassadeurs Bolt' driving with cars sticked with the Bolt logo.

+*Risks highlighted and comments*+:

We consider that the risk that would be the worst for us is definitely the +reclassification risk+, due to the financial consequences as well as the repercussions this could have (poor brand image, risk of other drivers suing us etc). Hence why we are mainly interested in assessing whether our proposed Solution 3 would lower the reclassification risks around 10-15% for the drivers driving with a car branded Bolt.

The risk of being sued by a passenger for +misleading advertising+ is also considerable and the sanctions are high. What we could envisage to mitigate such risk would be to add a sentence like '_Ceci est une publicité_' at the bottom of the Bolt logo, but in lower cases - big enough to be read from a passenger standing next to the car though. Note, this would probably require quite a lot of convincing for our CEO (though the associated sanctions will help) and therefore wouldn't necessarily be implemented at the same time as the new 'Solution' described above. Could we be sued as well by the DGCCRF for misleading advertising, or only by a passenger?

The risk of a driver suing us for +contract unbalanced / unfair+ seems also high, however the sanctions are not that high and I anticipate that the cost would be much lower for Bolt compared to the first 2 risks mentioned above.

I agree that there is also a risk of our competitors coming after us for +unfair practices+, but considering some of their practices, I don't deem that risk to be very high...  

I would be very grateful for your views on the above.

*Next steps:* Before reverting, could you please let me know where we stand as of today in terms of incurred fees with this assignment (phase 1), and what would you envisage in terms of fees for reverting on the questions above (and in the memo) - before instructing you to prepare the relevant documents for phase 2?

When calculating the total we do not have access to history data since we get it automatically from order-history. Thus, we have 2 options:

Option A. After Jan 1st the total will always be displayed in EUR - regardless of any order currency  - Pros: It is not confusing the user, that is how it works now

Overall behaviour:

* provider-portal: option A, all totals will be in EUR, regardless of any other currencies (he solution accepted by Kristina)
* provider-app: will go for option B, meaning that for totals before “Jan 1st”  the total should be like before, but after “Jan 1st” will only be displayed in EUR

Hi [~accountid:6284a37abd640f0068adea00] 

* *User requests a ride from his personal profile and receives an invoice without his VAT information (simplified invoice). If the user requests that his personal VAT information is added, we must perform this change. Would this be correct?* Yes, they have the right to ask for a complete invoice, to be able to recover the input VAT. 
* *User requests a ride from his personal profile and receives an invoice with or without his personal VAT information but wishes to change the name and VAT in the invoice to a company name and VAT. In other words, user requests a cross-entity change to the invoice. Are we obliged to perform this change by law?* Once an invoice is issued with the correct *and complete* data, it is not mandatory to change the invoice because the client decide to change the client name or addressee of the invoice. Therefore, if we have issued an invoice with all his personal VAT information, we are not obliged to rectify the invoice. Notwithstanding, if we have not included their personal VAT information, as passengers always can ask to include their data to be able to recover the input VAT, in this case it will not be a “new invoice” or a rectification of the invoice, as they can ask just to issue a complete invoice and replace their name for a company name with VAT information. So in my opinion is not the same if we have issued the invoices with or without his personal VAT information.

For baseline model I have used features below:

* recent waiting times, from last 10m, 1h, 4h, 1d, 7d and 28d
* same aggregated over 1st and 2nd ring for spatial smoothing
* marketplace forecasts
* surge
* time waves and other standard time features
* latitude, longitude

Used two model types to predict 10th and 90th quantile, without any category split:

* lasso as easily explainable baseline
* lgbm

The latter achieved better results even without tuning hyper-parameters in Tallinn, which proves there is much to gain from using lgbm over simple model.

Moving on to improving the lgbm model, with additional features, category information and finally tuning hyper-parameters.

Regarding splitting into categories: ideally we would split combinations into up to 3 groups, and the logic would be defined in config on per-city level. Having looked at percentages of drivers in different category groups a sensible split into 6 combinations could be:

# motorbike or cyclerickshaw
# autorickshaw (and no other at the same time)
# economy (and no other at the same time)
# economy_plus (whenever driver is listed in once of 4 cheap category groups above as well as one of more expensive categories listed below)
# standard (listed in standard or electric or taxi, also serving as default for weird points not matching anywhere else)
# standard_plus (listed in both standard and premium or comfort or xl/van/wav)

Those 6 groups will be furthered merged into 2-3, merging being controlled by config and a suggestion is below:

* Nairobi: 1 / 3 / the rest
* Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mwanza, Arusha: 1 / 2 / the rest
* Uyo: 2 / 3 / the rest
* whenever 1+2 is not empty: 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6
* otherwise, if 3 is significant: 3 / 4 / the rest (1,2 are expected to be empty)
* otherwise, if there is economy in the city: 3+4 / 5+1+2 / 6 (1,2 are expected to be empty)
* otherwise 1+2+3+4+5 / 6 (1,2,3,4 are expected to be empty)

The split is quite complex and I will work to simplify the general case. Specifically “3 is significant“ is very vague.

*Consent*
Withdrawing consent just influences the processing activities where we are using the legal bases of consent (User consent is just one potential legal basis for processing) Others are for example: necessary for a contract/legal obligation. As you see in our Bolt Privacy notice, most of the processing is happening  in order to provide the services contracted through the Bolt app with you.

*Data subject request*
Talking about keeping the data of the data subject:  By law we have to delete date if there is no legal ground for processing the information (Sec 3.1(9)): 

* no longer necessary for the purposes for which they were collected;
* withdrawn consent;
* the Data Subject objects to the processing and no overriding legitimate grounds;
* unlawfully processed; and
* for compliance with a legal obligation in Nigeria.

If we have to keep some data because of legal obligations (eg. accounting), than we do not have to delete them. BUT We are still storing the data and that's also why we have to give data subjects access to the stored data. (section 3.1 (5), (6) and (14))

The right to access, cannot be exercised if the request falls under the following circumstances:

* If the information requested contains information about other persons

* If the information is publicly available

* If a request has been complied with within a reasonable time frame and there have been no significant change in the information

* If opinions or references are given in confidence

Hello, the process is there: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4040950288/Requests+from+Authorities+or+Police|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4040950288/Requests+from+Authorities+or+Police|smart-link]

The reason we ask them to send also an email, while being on a call is minimal security check we should do. We need to be sure we release info to the police and directly to them. Pretending to be one and pressuring information to be released via phone is a known scam and this can have severe consequences. It shouldn't become a surprise to police that few extra steps is needed from them. And now we've a search option in Beehive which would make it easy to search and find the incoming email immediately. 

The process also states: _Otherwise, if the request does not indicate an immediate danger to life, always ask them to send a written DPA request including the below requirements to applicable_ [+_country/city email address_+|https://bolt.eu/en/cities/] _including their phone number._

So this means that if it truly is life or threat the agent needs to be sure of the officers identity (e.g pass certain security threshold) and in rare circumstances the info can be released over the phone. Regarding verification over the phone this depends on the market of what public info is available about the police, e.g  can agent call the officer back on a number published on the official police page? 

Regarding _usually, it gets to TIER1 outsourced agents who don't know what to do_ is something to be escalated to CS leadership and safety team as it’s an operational question and falls outside of privacy scope.

I re-thought how to approach weather data and build connections to CCPO. 

Wind (or rain) should be grouped according to their force guided by the official categorization thereof. E.g., wind force between 1-5 km/h is categorized as “light air”.

So what I did:

* Grouped wind force in Baku following [this|https://www.rmets.org/metmatters/beaufort-wind-scale] scale
* Removed all days where CS reported service disruption _not related to “bad weather”_ (payment issues, closed roads, etc.)
* Got a distribution of average CCPO in each group

Although not perfect, we now see a pattern where windy days trigger higher CCPO in the city.

!image-20221213-094945.png|width=603,height=248!

This is how it looks visually on the graph. Interestingly that on the day with most forceful wind, near gale, the CCPO was the lowest 🙄 But this might be an exception/data flaw, since it’s 1 day only.

!image-20221213-095115.png|width=801,height=502!

----

Applying the same logic for *Accra* but grouping by rainfall intensity, there is a pattern too. As rain intensifies, the CCPO goes up. 

Here we also have abnormalities - 2 days with violent rain had a lower CCPO than “no rain” days.

Another fact is that there might have been days with “other service disruption” which we don’t account for here.

!image-20221213-101155.png|width=511,height=186!

Visually, we can also see how “no rain” or “light rain” days have lower CCPO than days when rainfall was more intense.

Hey [~accountid:5e592fc3e7724a0e72644c61] thank you for the detailed ticket 🙏 

Let’s start from the top: 

{quote}Does this rule apply only to refunding the payment itself (refund to card)? Or could it be applied, if the eater is unhappy just with the compensation amount, but not with the compensation form?{quote}

This applies to *compensation form.* When and if we eventually get partial compensation to card, we will stop giving full refunds in this case. This is purely about Bolt not being within its legal rights to “make“ the user continue using the Bolt platform by giving them just credits. 

Refunds to cards should be given *only when the user explicitly requests them*, be it before or after any refunds were done. You can explain to the eater that card refunds take up to 2 weeks while Bolt Balance is there immediately, but nothing else should be said to dissuade eaters from card refunds in the cases where we are required to give them (all the articles have been updated) and in those cases card refunds *cannot be refused.* 

{quote} In this case, how should the CS communicate it? {quote}

Nothing special should be said. “We apologise for any inconvenience, the refund was sent to your card and should be visible in XY days” and so on should suffice. 

Regarding full refunds, again, *default is Bolt Balance*, if the user then says “No, I want it to card”, then and only then do you refund to card. 

{quote}Shall we then advise them, that the process works this way due to a legal obligation{quote}

Absolutely not. 

While it is great to see how much thought has gone into this from your side, the issue is quite simple - Eater requests refund to card, we have to give it. Eater requests full refund but doesn’t mention card, we don’t have to give it. It all boils down to them specifically saying “I want my refund done to my original payment method, I don’t want your credits”/ 

I would not complicate this process any more by adding any additional explanations without us having data that proves that these are real scenarios happening on the markets. 

Have an amazing week!

Ellex wrote the following memo:

_Please see below comments on possible agreements where Bolt Operations OÜ (_*_„Bolt Food“_*_) would restrict its partnering restaurants from purchasing services from Fudy OÜ (_*_„Fudy“_*_). Given the complexity of the issue, it could make sense to have a quick call on any questions._

*_In conclusion: (i) if/ when Bolt Food market shares are below 40% then Fudy specific restrictions on some restaurants could be used, but are in each case subject to analysis on the market situation; (ii) application of Fudy specific provisions if Bolt Food market share is above 40% will likely be considered as abuse of dominance (in practical terms only defence available would be to argue that Bold Food is not dominant)._* 

#  _Likely it is not feasible to draft clauses that can automatically be considered in compliance with competition law in all cases. Only basis for this could be if Bolt Food could rely on the vertical block exemption regulation (“_*_VBER_*_”). Likely this so-called safe harbour is not available:_

* _Currently, Bolt Food’s market share is above 30% (this automatically leads to non-application of VBER);_
* _If market shares are below 30%, then there is an argument that Fudy specific restrictions might be considered as restrictions on the use of online intermediaries (in effect restriction similar to parity clauses), which does not benefit from block exemption (VBER Article 5(1)(d)). Possible counterarguments to this could be found, but due to the relatively new regulation success cannot be guaranteed (see below for more details)._

_2.  Any use of Fudy specific clauses should be subject to case-by-case analysis, i.e. it is not automatically prohibited nor allowed. General rules to follow:_

* _Restrictions should not be used on must-carry partners, but instead partners which have a relatively small market share on Bolt Food and other platforms;_
* _There should be other non-restricted restaurants available in the same sub-segment with similar quality, pricing and other characteristics;_
* _Agreements should be relatively short (but could be prolonged once they end)._
* _Aim of these rules is to enable an argument that any applied restrictions do not have a material negative effect on competition._

*_3._*  +*_Market share above 40%:_*+ *_any restrictions are very risky and could be considered as abuse of dominance._* 

_Additional consideration: in case Bolt Food would apply Fudy specific clauses, then it is very likely that Fudy would complain to the Estonian Competition Authority (_*_ECA_*_). The ECA’s practice with online service providers has been contradictory and not fully in line with the guidelines/ practice of the Commission/ EU courts (e.g. the Wolt narrow-MFN case from 2021, which is in conflict with the current VBER). Also, as the market is currently concentrated (two larger players), then the presumption of the ECA will be that any clause against Fudy will lead to anti-competitive effects (incumbent largest undertaking takes steps to attempt to stop an entry of a new player). Hence, even after individual assessment risks with applying Fudy specific clauses exist._

_Our comments are explained in specific detail below._

 

+*_Vertical block exemption: likely not applicable_*+

_If it would be possible to rely on vertical block exemptions (as specified in the VBER) it would allow Bolt Food to conclude agreements with Fudy without a need to assess the competitive situation in each case. However, based on available information this will likely not be the case._

_·_       +_Market shares_+_: we understand that at the moment Bolt Food market share is estimated to be 51% (leaving open the market definition). Hence, VBER is not applicable due to said market share, if/ until market share is below 30%._ 

_·_       +_Even if market share is below 30%, it is not fully clear if applicability of VBER to Fudy specific clause would be excluded by VBER Article 5(1)(d)_+_:_

_o    It is likely that even though Fudy specific restriction is not a typical parity clause, then the ECA would likely argue that VBER Article 5(1)(d) is still applicable (economic effect of prohibition to use a platform is more severe than a parity clause)._

_o    At the same time, if the restriction is applied narrowly to Fudy, then it could be argued that the effect is similar to a narrow-parity clause (if at all) and VBER should still apply._

_o    Currently, VBER rules are new and no practice on the above is known._

_·       Other elements of the VBER: likely no other problems with relying on VBER will be relevant._

_o_      +_Prohibition is likely a non-compete obligation under VBER Article 5(1)(a)._+ _Solution duration of the agreement must have a defined duration below 5 years (or it is tacitly renewable in a way that the counterparty can truly exit the agreement)._

_o_      +_Likely the restrictions would not amount to breach of VBER Article 4(3)._+

_o_      +_Even if Bolt Food and restaurants are competing undertakings (which do an extent can be argued), then they could benefit from VBER Article 2(4)_+_, unless Bolt Food would like to apply restrictions to deliveries of groceries. For the sake of clarity, in case Bolt Food would run dark-kitchen type of services itself, it would be considered as a competing undertaking and could not benefit from VBER._

+*_Individual assessment: in case Bolt Food market share remains below 40%_*+

_For each agreement concluded an individual assessment should be carried out to be able to argue that concluded restriction would not lead to restriction on competition by effect. It is likely that with some restaurants restrictive agreements can be concluded._

_For background under TFEU Article 101(1) agreements, which have as their object or effect the prevention, restriction or distortion of competition, are prohibited. For agreements that restrict competition by object no effects analysis is needed._

_·_           +_Likely Fudy-specific or wider clause would not amount to by object restriction (that is it is not automatically prohibited)._+ _The concept of restriction by object relates to agreements that by their very nature are harmful to the functioning of normal competition (Commission´s notice on the application of Article 101(3) of TFEU, recital 21). This encompasses behaviour where the anti-competitive effects of an agreement can be expected already from (i) nature of the agreement, (ii) experience or (iii) high potential for damage. Recent ECJ practice has limited the cases where by object infringement can be argued for. Typically exclusivity agreements are not considered to have anticompetitive object. Excluding only one competitor has even smaller effects on the competition._ *_Hence, it should also not constitute an infringement by object_*_. Please note that the ECA has in the past argued that exclusivity agreements are by object breaches and in the 2021 Wolt related narrow-MFN clause the ECA in effect argued that such clause is a by object restriction. EU practice (including new vertical restraints guidelines) would help to counter the views of the ECA._

_·_           +_Possible appreciable effect on competition._+ _Based on the above, the agreement would only be prohibited, if it materially restricts competition on the market, that is in each case analysis on market situation would be needed._ 

_o     To assess the possible anti-competitive effects of restrictions on the use of online marketplace(-s), it would be important to show that (i) other online platforms have options still available to compete (i.e. other platforms could conclude agreements with other restaurants and build up a mix of restaurants that the users would expect to see on the platform); (ii) no must have restaurants are excluded by restrictions; (iii) restrictions are of relatively short duration._

_o     Said actual alternatives should be documented and no wide effect on competition should be clearly demonstratable. From practical perspective the ECA is likely to consider any directly anti-Fudy agreements as having (at least some) negative effects on the competition as it is directed at a new entrant to the market._

_o     Likely it will not be possible to present any arguments whereby Fudy specific clause has pro-competitive effects. Also, we do not consider it likely that any efficiency defences are available._

 

+*_Dominance_*+

_Given the current market structure (two large food platforms Wolt and Bolt Food), it is  possible to argue that Bolt Food is not dominant – both platforms have approximately equal market share. At the same time, there has been one case in the ECA practice where an undertaking with a market share of 50%+ has been considered as not dominant._

_Therefore, as long as Bold Food has a market share of above 40% it should be assumed that it has a dominant position. Under the Estonian Competition Act § 13(1) dominance is presumed if an undertaking holds a market share more than 40% (in practice it is difficult to overturn this presumption)._

_Restricting the use of Fudy for restaurants (or exclusivity clauses in general) would constitute as limiting service/ goods markets and imposing ancillary obligations which have no connection with the subject of the agreement. Given the earlier ECA practice it would be very difficult to argue that clauses directed at Fudy would not amount to abuse of dominance, e.g. the ECA argued that an abuse of dominance existed for agreements requiring exclusivity for a single event (ECA decision of 9 September 2019 No nr 5-5/2019-050 – AS Piletilevi)._ 

_Until Bolt Food has a market share exceeding 40% the only defence available (in case of investigations) would be that Bold Food is not dominant. Success of said defence is questionable._

 

+*_Other elements to consider_*+

* _Use of direct and clear anti-Fudy clauses most probably lead to complaints to the ECA. Hence, Bolt Food should be certain of its case prior to seeking to agree on such clauses. For practical purposes it could make sense to consider using practices that are not directed directly towards Fudy._
* _If Fudy has exclusive agreements with Apollo related restaurants, then one could consider analysing if Fudy/ Apollo form a single economic unit. If this is not the case, then there could be an argument that such exclusivity set-ups could be illegal. For this the market share of Fudy should arise above 15% as otherwise the agreements could potentially benefit from de-minimis provisions. At the same time, if Fudy/ Apollo do form a same economic unit, then said agreements would be considered as intragroup transactions and thereby allowed. Based on available information there seems to be a shareholder structure in play. Hence, we should have good arguments for claiming that said exclusivity agreements are anti-competitive (once market shares rise somewhat)._  
* _Just in case, our memorandum dated 22 October 2022 is not up-to date anymore due to new EU level regulations._

2. Transfer-Acceptance Act/Delivery note  (not really important how we call it)
- If TAA has major defects, Commencement Date is postponed, and we should set new Delivery Date.
- If TAA has minor defects, Commencement Date stays the same and we sign TAA.

3. “Commencement Date” - means the date on which the Lessee commences the use of the Premises, from that date the Lessee is obliged to comply with all conditions set out in this Agreement, including obligation relating to the payment of the Base Rent

- If Delivery Date is postponed due to the Landloard fault, Commencment Date is postponed. We stay in our old premises, and wait for new Delivery date, don’t pay rent (both old office and new office).
- If Delivery Date is postponed due to our fault - Commencment Date stay the same. We stay in our old premises, and wait for new Delivery date, we pay for old office and new office.

I talked to Food Delivery Supportability and this was the conclusion of the discussion:

* This does not have to be limited only to delays caused by couriers - sometimes the restaurants accept way more orders than they can realistically make in a timely manner. Even though our T&C state that the ETAs are not binding, it is logical that if the ETA displayed is 20-30 mins and the order ends up taking 90 mins that something went wrong and the eater wouldn’t have ordered from the restaurant if they knew how long the order would end up taking.
* However, at the moment we don’t have data to decide where to draw the line - what should be considered a delay long enough to warrant the order being cancelled?
* Supportability has data showing that the issue described in the original ticket is of negligent importance and the conversations that would have to take place to decide on a time frame where cancellations are allowed would be complicated and would not be able to happen in the next few months (due to planning 2023 and kicking the year off).
* Supportability, Product, OPS and Content will look into issues related to order delays and order cancellations in 2023 (we need to figure out the logic then e.g. do we cancel at all? which part do we automate? how do we support with manual processes?)
* The part about leaving a note on the customer profile when the order is cancelled due to severe delays has been deleted from the article (so that the customer is not denied in the future if they request another order cancellation) and this is going to be the only action taken at this moment in time.

Hi Diana,

Being able to see the payslips is not part of a scheduled integration. Instead, it is based on an adhoc API functionality that triggers every time any Danish employee searches for ‘My Payslips’ in Workday. Their Payslips page will open, which sends out a call to Immedis to display the payslip lines and files. Once they are made available in Immedis, they should immediately appear. If they do not, please first reach out to your Payroll team to ensure that nothing went wrong on Immedis' side, as we in the Workday team cannot help you with that. Once Immedis confirms that all is well on their end, your payroll provider will raise it with us to investigate any possible outages and/or failures.

*Resolution*:

Simply type “My Payslips” into the searchbar of Workday, and select the first option. Wait a few seconds for the API to do its thing, and you should see a response. Either the lines will be visible, or “No payslips were found” will be shown, in which case your country specific Payroll expert should investigate.

Kind regards,
Tim Tuinstra

It’s not just event loop lag, but also:
* ‘thundering herd effect’ with huge spikes of network load when IMDS is updated and many services try to fetch the data at the same time.
[https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C049U1GKWQN/p1669383695143809?thread_ts=1669383680.512669&cid=C049U1GKWQN|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C049U1GKWQN/p1669383695143809?thread_ts=1669383680.512669&cid=C049U1GKWQN|smart-link]
We had to upscale servers that are otherwise under-utilized for this.

* As we grow, payload will grow and at some point parsing it may not fit into the timeout if performance of something (service, network) temporarily degrades:

{quote}system-data-geo-resolver: Has 7MB responses if client can not retrieve the response in 8 seconds, the client will retry and keep retrying infinitely causing a feedback loop which will bring down our services. The response time will keep increasing and increasing - overloading Envoy and it will not stop since there is no exponential backoff strategy on the client side.{quote}

[https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C038Z5BEC1J/p1670407824837009|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C038Z5BEC1J/p1670407824837009|smart-link]

After thorough discussions with the OPS team and careful evaluation, I concluded that the requested CS process brings little value. 

The parallel CS process would bring value only if:

* we call the user, and they pick up (if they don’t, we can’t know when they’d respond to the in-app message, if ever - so here, it’s best for OPS to just react to the alert and go and check the car)
* the user can tell CS something about the particular situation that OPS wouldn’t find out by inspecting the car.

It sounds like quite a complicated collaboration between CS and OPS, where the CS are middlemen, and users are very likely to provide us with nothing valuable when we’d call them. With the above stated, at the moment, I don’t see much value in creating this CS process. I’m happy to be proven otherwise, though. 🙂

Hi [~accountid:6284a37abd640f0068adea00] - sorry for the delay in getting back to you on this.

There is not going to be a legal ‘cut off’ after which passengers are *_not_* entitled to refunds - the legal limitation period for beaches of contract tends to be *many years* in most countries. This will generally the same for rides and food. However, we should be more cautious with rides as that sector is more heavily regulated.

Of course, here we’re talking about our customer service responses rather than deadlines for legal proceedings. The problem is that it may be very difficult to verify the nature of the complaint after the passage of time - the driver/courier is not going to remember any specific journey several months down the line.

I would suggest as follows:

(1) if the complaint regards *serious misconduct* by the driver, we *always* investigate.
(2) if the complaint relates to something that is easily verifiable by Bolt internally (i.e. the trip didn’t even happen at all) then we can investigate internally and proceed to remedy the passenger if necessary.
(3) if a complaint concerns behaviour that (A) is disputable, (B) it cannot be verified without discussing with the driver, (C) the complaint is poorly formulated AND (D) it does *_not_* relate to passenger safety, then we have scope to say the following (or a variation thereof): 

_“It is very important that all complaints in respect of journeys are made to Bolt promptly so that this can be properly investigated. Unfortunately, due to the passage of time, Bolt is unable to verify the circumstances and we’re therefore unable to consider your request for a refund.”_

Keep in mind though that there will always be scope for customers to keep pushing for refunds and eventually take legal action if they are particularly aggrieved. Bolt therefore needs to consider each complaint on its merits - the longer the time gap between the complaint and the ride, the more scope we will have to say that too much time has passed and we cannot verify the complaint.

I hope that helps, any further Qs just let me know - thanks 👌

[^EU_Nov_2022_driver_data_v2.csv]

{noformat}select 
asc2.country_code as market,
iii.client_vat as market_vat,
ROUND(SUM(COALESCE( CASE WHEN cot.state in ('finished', 'client_cancelled', 'client_did_not_show')  then cot.ride_price else 0 END,0)),0) as gmv_loc,
count(distinct case when fd.invoice_issuer_reg_code != fc.reg_code and fd.invoice_issuer_vat_code != fc.vat_code then cot.driver_id end) as total_active_private_drivers,
count(distinct case when fd.invoice_issuer_reg_code != fc.reg_code and fd.invoice_issuer_vat_code != fc.vat_code and fd.invoice_issuer_is_liable_to_vat = true then cot.driver_id end) as vat_liable_private_drivers,
count(distinct case when fd.invoice_issuer_reg_code != fc.reg_code and fd.invoice_issuer_vat_code != fc.vat_code and fd.invoice_issuer_is_liable_to_vat = false then cot.driver_id end) as no_vat_liable_private_drivers,
count(distinct case when fd.invoice_issuer_reg_code = fc.reg_code and fd.invoice_issuer_vat_code = fc.vat_code then cot.driver_id end) as total_active_fleet_drivers,
count(distinct case when fd.invoice_issuer_reg_code = fc.reg_code and fd.invoice_issuer_vat_code = fc.vat_code and fc.is_liable_to_vat = true then cot.driver_id end) as vat_liable_fleet_drivers,
count(distinct case when fd.invoice_issuer_reg_code = fc.reg_code and fd.invoice_issuer_vat_code = fc.vat_code and fc.is_liable_to_vat = false then cot.driver_id end) as no_vat_liable_fleet_drivers
from glue.ng_public.fleet_driver fd 
left join glue.ng_public.company_order_try cot on cot.driver_id = fd.id
left join glue.ng_public.fleet_company fc on fc.id = fd.company_id 
left join glue.ng_public.admin_system_city asc2 on asc2.id = cot.city_id 
left join (select country, client_vat, state from glue.ng_public.invoicing_invoice_issuer group by 1,2,3) iii on iii.country = asc2.country_code and iii.state = 'active'
where DATE(cot.price_review_finished_timestamp) >= DATE('2022-11-01') and DATE(cot.price_review_finished_timestamp) <= DATE('2022-11-30')
and asc2.country_code in ( 'at', 'be', 'bg', 'hr', 'cy', 'cz', 'dk', 'ee', 'fi', 'fr', 'de', 'gr', 'hu', 'ie', 'it', 'lv', 'lt', 'lu', 'mt', 'nl', 'pl', 'pt', 'ro', 'sk', 'si', 'es', 'se')

Having had a closer look at the data I found the following:

* categories 1 and 2 are very different in avg waiting time to other categories and between them, suggesting it is never sensible to merge them
* categories 5 and 6 are very similar, in some cities 6 has lower avg waiting times, but in other higher, suggesting a lot of noise. found little evidence in splitting them bringing extra information, so will merge them for v1
* categories 3 and 4 are sometimes ok to merge (usually when 3 is small in size) and sometimes not

I will suggest a following split, with same logic for all cities:

* 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 5+6

The only downside is that there are 5 category combinations rather than 3, but it will boil down to 1-3 in most cases. In fact I only found 8 cities with 4 combinations and 2 with 5 combinations (based on one week in August '22). Among those 10, only 3 have significant (>1%) amount of data in each group. I believe it’s better to maintain up to 5 combinations with simple logic than to maintain combination-picking logic.

We would still want the ability to pick any subset of the 5 combinations in the config file. Should any combination be excluded in the config, but present in the data, I suggest not serving waiting times to the excluded group (a more complicated alternative would be to define backup combination, for example if group 3 is excluded in config, but present in data, use 5 instead). Should any combination be present in the config, but missing in the data (or having very few data points), I would still suggest not serving. The model as currently designed would be capable of serving predictions, but I would not trust those and improving on that axis isn’t worth it, as model will be regularly retrained and as soon as it sees some data, it will start serving reliable predictions.

*Replacing per-vehicle features in rental_fleet with per-vehicle disabled features in rentl_car_vehicle*

All vehicles in live that have any per-vehicle features +enabled+ also have these features enabled for their models. So the migration from rental_fleet.car_vehicle_*feature*_link to rental_car_vehicle.vehicle_*disabled_feature*_link looks pretty straightforward.

The query to check this attached below:

{noformat}select
    model.display_name, f.name_default,
    if(exists(select 0 from car_vehicle_model_feature_link mod_link where mod_link.feature_id = veh_link.feature_id and car.model_id = mod_link.model_id), 'yes', 'no') as redundant
from car_vehicle_feature_link veh_link
    join car_vehicle_feature f on f.id = veh_link.feature_id
    join car_vehicle car on car.id = veh_link.vehicle_id
    join car_vehicle_model model on model.id = car.model_id
where veh_link.is_active = 1;{noformat}

*Michael Roberts'* reply from Legal team on [+LSS-15045+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/47/LSS-15045]: 

Hi - sorry for the delay in getting back to you on this.

There is not going to be a legal ‘cut off’ after which passengers are *_not_* entitled to refunds - the legal limitation period for beaches of contract tends to be *many years* in most countries. This will generally the same for rides and food. However, we should be more cautious with rides as that sector is more heavily regulated.

Of course, here we’re talking about our customer service responses rather than deadlines for legal proceedings. The problem is that it may be very difficult to verify the nature of the complaint after the passage of time - the driver/courier is not going to remember any specific journey several months down the line.

I would suggest as follows:

(1) if the complaint regards *serious misconduct* by the driver, we *always* investigate.
(2) if the complaint relates to something that is easily verifiable by Bolt internally (i.e. the trip didn’t even happen at all) then we can investigate internally and proceed to remedy the passenger if necessary.
(3) if a complaint concerns behaviour that (A) is disputable, (B) it cannot be verified without discussing with the driver, (C) the complaint is poorly formulated AND (D) it does *_not_* relate to passenger safety, then we have scope to say the following (or a variation thereof):

_“It is very important that all complaints in respect of journeys are made to Bolt promptly so that this can be properly investigated. Unfortunately, due to the passage of time, Bolt is unable to verify the circumstances and we’re therefore unable to consider your request for a refund.”_

Keep in mind though that there will always be scope for customers to keep pushing for refunds and eventually take legal action if they are particularly aggrieved. Bolt therefore needs to consider each complaint on its merits - the longer the time gap between the complaint and the ride, the more scope we will have to say that too much time has passed and we cannot verify the complaint.

I hope that helps, any further Qs just let me know - thanks 👌

Result of investigation


*UPD*: on why the delivery matching didn't recover in a timely manner after the incident was resolved on platform level*Context*:
The order matching is a cron with Global Lock that is configured to run every 10 seconds with a timeout of 60 seconds.
This cron is fetching data about courier assignment for every city and for every city computes the data that needs to be processed:

# orders to be failed - long period of time of no matching
# orders to be matched  - orders that need to have a courier assigned

The data gathered in the getDataSet() is then processed in a parallel manner with a 5 parallel degree which in normal conditions it takes less than a couple of seconds,*During the incident* the getDataSet was not able to fetch the courier & provider details which made the cron to not being able to compute the data that needs to be processed.*After the incident* (proxysql being fixed):
The cron stayed with the lock on the same machine.
The services called by the cron now started to respond properly but the getDataSet() duration was very big.
This caused the getDataSet() method of the cron to take more than the cron timeout duration of 60 seconds.
Because of this the cron run was aborted and no matching was done even though the data was computed. This behaviour can be seen by the fact that there are a lot of logs with {{Lost local lock, aborting run.}}What is observed is that the service context switches were very high.
Why this happened sample:

# cron run starts at second 0
# all the next crons runs (5 are not starting because of lock being taken)
# the 6th cron run takes the lock an theoretically 2 cron runs are getting data set in parallel
# so depending on how long the getDataSet was taking we could end up with 3-4 instances getting the same date which kill the performance.

After the incident happening on the 12th of December we restarted our service which forced the cron to move to another instance that helped the *getDataSet()* to happen faster from over 60 seconds to just 15 seconds which allowed cron to start consuming the data. This because on the fresh instance the it was running just a single instance of getDataSet*Action items*

* move the logic from a cron architecture to a event based one

* have the cron just emitting the events and workers to process them to avoid any possible scenarios like this

* another possible short term solution would be increasing the timeout duration of that cron

Hi [~accountid:62c53aac7273faf658f10f90] Due the reclassification risk, our recommendation is not to use acceptance rates in campaigns.

Here is the memo concerning this issue [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rXJFA8_V5EbCK6pIi3HxuzXmF0r5yR1r-Xk017zIHGs/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rXJFA8_V5EbCK6pIi3HxuzXmF0r5yR1r-Xk017zIHGs/edit|smart-link]

*Conclusions*

# *Bonuses should not be based on acceptance rates as this increases the likelihood of a reclassification risk.* 

This view is based on a Spanish case relating to Glovo in which it was found to have exercised control over drivers by providing higher income to those who worked ‘high value’ time slots. Whilst similar cases are not currently live in other countries it is likely that the Glovo case will be taken into consideration as reclassification in the gig economy is currently being reviewed at EU level as part of the Platform Workers Directive. The use of acceptance rates by Bolt would set a potentially damaging precedent.

# *Guidelines and recommendations for applying performance bonuses*

* The idea scenario is: “*Do X (number of finished orders), get Y (fixed fee)*”.
* Where an ideal scenario is not possible (or business need is very high): “*Do X in period Y get Z*”. Time period should be longer rather than shorter (i.e. daily rather than hourly - “Do X within an hour” for example is far less defensible than “Do X over the weekend”) and targets should be demonstrably achievable (based on actual data). In addition to reclassification risks, shorter time periods also increase the likelihood of accidents related to the couriers. 
* There should be no or very limited negative consequences for the courier (e.g. blocking; decreased rating; limiting the courier’s freedom in any other way, e.g. limiting access to the best time slots, etc) for rejecting the orders/low acceptance rate.
* Campaigns should be carried out on random days, maximum 1-2 days a week.
* Other performance metrics (on-time delivery, etc) should be avoided. Emphasis should be put on the number of finished orders instead.
* Terms such as “bonuses”, “compensation”, “online hours”, “guarantees”, “minimum earnings”, “guaranteed earnings” should be avoided. 

Hope this helps. Pls let me know if you have any questions

This will include the readable name and also include the geojson object id for easier and non-ambiguous referencing.

Similarly to get the micromobility parking area polygons the following query can be used: [https://geodata.bymoslo.no/arcgis/rest/services/geodata/ELsparkesykler_Visning/MapServer/3/query?where=1%3D1&outFields=*&f=geojson|https://geodata.bymoslo.no/arcgis/rest/services/geodata/ELsparkesykler_Visning/MapServer/3/query?where=1%3D1&outFields=*&f=geojson]
